Showcase Day 2022

Showcase Day 2022 took place on Sunday 29 May

Showcase Day is an annual event for Patrons where you can get closer to behind the scenes theatre-making at the RSC. This year the event was held in the Royal Shakespeare Theatre with a number of really exciting panels and workshops. The structure of the day followed the process of what an actor would experience working at the Royal Shakespeare Company, from rehearsals to opening night. The day was split into different workshops, panels and discussions.


Panel Discussion- The Rehearsal Room Experience

This discussion was chaired by Nicky Cox, speaking with actors Jonathan Broadbent, Hannah Young, Jamie Wilkes, Keith Osborn and Stage Manager Jen Davey. 'The Rehearsal Room Experience' Panel centred around the experiences of an actor working at the RSC. The creatives have personal experience working with the RSC, giving us an actor's insight into the production we see on stage.


Delving into the Text; An In Conversation around the 37 Plays project

Acting Artistic Director Erica Whyman chatted to Juliet Gilkes Romero (The Whip, The Day of The Living) and Mark Ravenhill (The Boy in The Dress, Candide, RSC Writer in Residence). Focusing on the process of writing, inspiration, and the beginnings of a play, this panel was a call to action for everyone and anyone to write something for the 37 Plays project.


Exploring the Voice, with RSC Voice Practitioner Ellen Hartley

During this workshop, Ellen explored how actors' voices are kept healthy at the RSC, and offered the opportunity to stand on stage to warm up the voice and experiment with acoustics and projection. This workshop focused on the practical and physical aspects of being an actor here at the RSC. 


Putting on a Costume: a Demonstration from RSC Running Wardrobe

Running Wardrobe technicians Jennifer Williams and Rebecca Rees talked in depth about their work. This demonstration focused on the behind the scenes work that many are not aware of. This demonstration also included a test of quick changes, where Jennifer and Rebecca dressed and undressed Nicky Cox in armour, to test their quick change skills in front of an audience. 


An Insight into a Technical Rehearsal

Head of Sound Jeremy Dunn and Head of Lighting Kevin Sleep talked about the importance and impacts of light and sound on a stage. In the final demonstration of the day, we were able to see the development of a show once it has gone into technical rehearsal, with the use of light and sound having a huge impact on an audience's experience of the production. Jeremy and Kevin used a variety of different effects to try and explore the different atmospheres which could be represented on stage. 

This event was a lovely insight into the life of an actor and the way they experience the Royal Shakespeare Company from a professional perspective.

webpage.text:
From Mark Borchardt to Bon Iver, Wisconsin Film Festival achieves peak Wisconsin | Movies

Mark Borchardt. Beer. Michael Feldman. Hummingbird feeders. Chippewa Falls. Bon Iver. The Crystal Corner Bar.

The 19th Annual Wisconsin Film Festival may have achieved peak Wisconsin on its opening night Thursday night at the Barrymore Theatre.

The festival has typically used its opening night slot to highlight a big, crowd-pleasing film to pack a big theater like the Barrymore. But this time, festival programmers opted to highlight its strong selection of Wisconsin-made films.

“We’ll have many, many exceptional films from around the world to see over the next seven days,” festival coordinator Ben Reiser said. “But tonight, the Wisconsin Film Festival is all about Wisconsin."

After handing out Golden Badger Awards to several local filmmakers (including 65 fourth-graders at Crestwood Elementary who made a stop-motion animated film about the myth of Daedalus and Icarus), the festival settled in for four short documentaries set in Wisconsin, collectively titled “Transmissions From the Heartland.”

Christina Ciano and Jeff Buss’ “A Place in the Garden” is a lovely and vibrant doc about two Wisconsin couples, including Michael and Kathi Rock of Madison, who have turned their backyards into little hummingbird sanctuaries. Besides showing us up-close-and-personal footage of hummingbirds (including an epic throwdown over a feeder), it’s a gentle ode to Wisconsinites and their flying friends.

Next came a not-so-gentle ode to Wisconsinites and their flying friends. “The Dundee Project” is the long-awaited film from Milwaukee filmmaker Mark Borchardt, perhaps best known as the subject of the 2000 documentary “American Movie.” For “Dundee,” Borchardt traveled up to UFO Days at Benson’s Hide-A-Way Bar in Milwaukee, where the locals sit by the lake, drink beer and wait for the unidentified flying objects to show up.

The gap between Borchardt’s flowery narration (he calls the bar owner “the centrifugal figure of all things byzantine”) and the tottering local denizens on screen is a hoot, especially a character named UFO Bob who insists that the aliens like to come to Wisconsin to tune into Green Bay Packers games. The film was saved from being mean-spirited by Borchardt’s earnest and generous presence in front of and behind the camera.

During the post-show Q&A, Borchardt was all one would have hoped he would be, peppering his answers with profanities and “dudes,” and at one point asking a questioner, “How are you doing, man?” When Borchardt took a selfie with “Whad’ya Know?” host Michael Feldman, it felt like the Badger State’s own “Batman vs. Superman: Dawn of Justice” moment when titans join forces.


Feldman was there for “Whad’ya Do Now?," Marc Kornblatt’s documentary about Feldman ending his longtime radio show (against his will) after 31 years. Feldman is his wry, sardonic self as always, with no small bitterness against Wisconsin Public Radio honchos for pulling the plug after 31 years. But he’s also surprisingly vulnerable, and his delight in having taken the show all over the country and finding funny, quirky, friendly folks everywhere is contagious.


Kornblatt’s film ends with the final radio show at Shannon Hall last June. I think it would have been stronger to show more of Feldman’s attempt to transition into podcasting, including continuing shows at the High Noon Saloon. The next one, by the way, is noon Saturday.


My favorite film of the quartet was Andrew Swant’s “Silently Steal Away,” a film about the mysterious “Jack Raymond Show” that emanates from a small independent radio station in Chippewa Falls. Each night, listeners within WCFW’s broadcast area hear the dulcet tones of Raymond as he plays Percy Faith and Herb Alpert tunes and dispenses jokes and wisdom culled from the pages of Reader’s Digest. Swant pairs audio of the easy listening show with footage of snowplows braving a Wisconsin winter, an unlikely marriage that somehow fits like a glove.

The show has drawn superfans of the likes of Justin Vernon of Bon Iver, who gravitate to its singular, weird charm in an increasingly corporatized radio world (which Feldman knows all too well). But who is, or was, Raymond? Swant investigates, and the answers feel quintessentially Wisconsin, an ode to a small, out-of-the-way pocket of the state where strange magic can happen to those savvy enough to tune into its wavelength.

The Wisconsin Film Festival runs through Sunday at the Barrymore Theatre and several theaters on the UW-Madison campus, and through next Thursday at Sundance Cinemas. For a complete schedule, visit 2017.wifilmfest.org.

webpage.text:
Films of yesteryear: A Q&A with Ron Robinson Theater manager Joey Cole

If you like movies and Ron Robinson Theater isn’t on your radar, what exactly are you doing? Since 2014, the 315-seat downtown venue run by the Central Arkansas Library System has rarely strayed from being the best, cheapest and most consistent place in town to watch films of yesteryear on the big screen. These days, Ron Robinson offers more than a dozen unique showings per month, most of which are priced at only $5 plus fees. 

What’s more, the selection is always eclectic, spanning a century of film history and ranging from the critically acclaimed and widely beloved to the obscure and culty. Who, I’ve wondered for years, is behind this quirky and impressive operation?

Theater Manager Joey Cole, that’s who. Cole, who spoke with us in July, joined the team at Ron Robinson in 2018 after several years in academia at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock and Pulaski Technical College. 

What’s your curating philosophy and what kind of priorities are you balancing when you put together the film lineup each month?

It’s a weird combination of many things. Mary [Osteen], who is upstairs currently, is also involved in this process. It’s one part research, studying films, film trends, how they’ve done at the box office in the past, their cult status. I do have to fight against my own tastes because while some fall into that category, I try not to just do films I like, but films that I think people would be excited about seeing on the big screen. 

At the end of the day, what we’re trying to do is nostalgia. That’s the biggest component, which is why typically 20 years old is the line. Right now, 2006 is about as young of a film that we’ll go. We break it here and there to see what would happen, but the general philosophy is to lean into the classics as much as possible. 

Everybody that I talk to — and you’re going to be included in that, by the way — I ask for their thoughts, suggestions, desires. We’ve made Facebook posts. I’ve got a board up in the office with post-its, and whenever anyone says, “Have you thought about showing this?” I stick it up there. 

The latest trend I’ve done is looking at anniversaries quite a bit, which is pretty noticeable, because you’ll see 40th anniversary of this, 55th anniversary of that. It seems like that’s always an opportunity to get people’s eyeballs and attention a little more. 

Does the process of securing film rights play a role in what ends up showing at Ron Robinson? Are some movies more of a challenge than others to screen?

Definitely. There’s a lot of different entities that I deal with directly to get the rights, depending on who has a film, and mainly it’s by distributor. So whenever I’m looking at or talking about a film, you might see me look to see who’s the distributor. Universal Warner Brothers — pretty easy. Fox Films — pretty easy. Those are all just an email and it’s more or less the same price for all the films. Criterion, which does all of the 20th Century Fox Films, fluctuates a bit in price, but there’s no rhyme or reason to it. Sometimes, you’ve gotta play “who has the rights today” for films that have changed hands. The big variances come with things like “Star Wars,” which is stupid expensive to book.

It’s more complicated when you get to some of the more obscure things we book. “Sharknado,” for example, was never made to be in theaters really, so the rights owners are like, “OK, what are you doing with other people?” 

When we did “Sharkansas Women’s Prison Massacre,” I actually reached out directly to the director and I’m like, “Hey, I’m trying to find the rights to this film,” and he’s like, “Actually, I have the rights to that one.”

The problem is when you hit a stumbling block, like “Oh, sorry, that film’s in moratorium, you can’t have the rights.”

What does “moratorium” mean?

More often than not, it’s when the studios are going to do some major re-release themselves, or Fathom [Entertainment] has acquired the rights, and they’re going to do a major re-release, which means none of us can get the rights for a while. 

Or if a new “Avengers” movie is coming out, then any title that carries the name “Avengers” has been pulled. They don’t want attention drawn away from this product. They want all eyes here. “The Wiz” was pulled when “Wicked” was coming out because Universal didn’t want another Universal product competing with “Wicked.” 

Multiple screenings a month at Ron Robinson are billed as “BingoFlix.” What’s that all about?

People love it. If I get to say, “Yay, we created something awesome,” it’s this. Other people around the country have done similar things and I didn’t just invent it out of nowhere, but I brought it here and created what it is now. Essentially, I’ve literally got a list of about 70 movie cliches that I can find in just about every film. Explosion. Falls while running. Wall is really a door. Some are genre-related, so they may not be in every film, which is good, because then you can use those calls for fake filler spaces on the cards. 

When it started, it was a very small but dedicated crowd. We had maybe seven or eight people at that first one. Then it started to grow, and then grew some more and then grew some more. Now, we have what I call the “BingoFlix bump.” I can take any film and make it into a BingoFlix and we’ll get at least 50 more people coming who are just like, “We’re here for the bingo. We don’t care what the film is.”

I used to make all the cards be winners, but I broke the bank when we did “National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation” and had 215 people come. It was a madhouse of prizes flying everywhere. We created such a clog coming in and out of the theater. It was fun, great mayhem, but that was the moment when the team was like, “Maybe everyone should not be winning.” 

The prize table is quite eclectic. I think the first prize ever was an Elvis Presley eight-track. We’ve had everything from big planters and a sink to free tickets and sponsored gifts like jewelry or discounted stuff at places. 

Another recurring event is the monthly screening of “The Rocky Horror Picture Show.” Is that still vibrant these days? 

We average around 70 people. I’ve always been a big believer in it, for a lot of reasons. The community that is built in it, of it, around it. Its enduring popularity. It was something that I thought was the greatest thing when I was younger and sought it out. It’s a very inclusive movie and audience. 

During the pandemic, some folks moved here from Seattle — Steve and Andrea Singleton — and they heard we were doing it monthly. He was a big time participant in the Seattle, Portland area, and he’s like, “Hey, what would you think about doing a pre-show? I’ll do it. I’ll take care of everything.” I had been struggling to do cool things on top of all of this. I would do the cheer and announcements and birthdays, basically copying what happens on stage in the 1980 movie “Fame.” But he’s like, “I’ll put together this full thing.” So we started working on that together, and he recruited some folks, and now each month it’s a full blown 30-minute pre-show with games and contests and prizes. 

We sell prop bags because I remember how difficult it was to get all the props and get ready to go to the movie. I remember I spent the better part of the entire day on a Saturday running around getting cards and bread and rice when I was young. I’ve already done all that work for everyone. 

What about the Exhibition on Screen and National Theatre Live events? Are those harder to get people to come out to?

Exhibition on Screen is out of control. It has one of the highest regular attendances. 100, 150 people, pretty much on the regular. You can only get so close to certain things at an exhibit or museum, and here, it’s up close and you’re looking at it and they’re discussing it. You get really immersed in the art in such a way that you just can’t experience any other way.  

National Theatre Live is still trying to find its way a little more. The way they film it and the way that they produce it, it gives you the feeling that you’re right there, but some of those have super long run times — like three hours — and Exhibition on Screen is typically a tight hour and 30 minutes.

If readers have movies they want to recommend for screening at Ron Robinson, what’s the best way for them to share that with you?

Email ronrobinsontheater@cals.org or email me directly at jcole@cals.org. Or send us a Facebook message or comment.

JMArts—Pinnacle of the Arts 

Experiencing World-Class Art.
Learning from World-Class Artists.
All Free to JM Students.

Pinnacle of the Arts gives JM actors, artists, dancers and musicians an opportunity to experience world-class arts and learn directly from world-class artists. About 15 to 30 students attend each event entirely free of charge. That includes excellent seating locations, transportation and even lunch or dinner, often at school before the journey begins. And thanks to generous contributions from our partners — including the Wren Foundation — this entire series is offered free of charge.

2024-25 PINNACLE OF THE ARTS: A LOOK BACK
a few scenes from last year’s inaugural series


WHAT KIND OF EVENTS DO YOU OFFER?


what world-class artists do students meet?


We work very hard to arrange time during each event for JM artists to meet world-class artists and learn about the work they’re experiencing. At the North Carolina Museum of Art, that meant behind-the-scenes access with professionals on staff to learn about key works on exhibit and how the art is obtained, presented and preserved. For performances, that often includes private conversations with artists who are performing.

Here are some of the artists who met with students in our most recent season. (There are some photos in the gallery above.)

 * “Hamilton.” Broadway actors Alex Nicholson and Sabrina Harrison

 * Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra with Wynton Marsalis. Bass player Carlos Henriquez

 * Behind the Scenes at the North Carolina Museum of Art. Head Librarian Andrew Wang

 * Handel’s “Messiah”. Vocal soloists alto/mezzo soprano Taylor Raven and tenor Aaron Crouch

 * Kotis Street Art Experience. Professional muralist and street artist Jenna Rice and street art patron Marty Kotis


WHO ARE ThE PARTNERS WHO MAKE THIS FREE FOR STUDENTS?


Glad you asked, because we’re honored to work with so many outstanding individuals and organizations who have been generous contributors to our work over the years. For the 2026-27 Pinnacle of the Arts series, we were blessed to welcome back partners who last year helped us create our inaugural season:

 * The Wren Foundation

 * Pate & Associates Marketing (Chip and Rose Pate)

The number and kinds of events we offer each year depends on our partners. So, if you are interested in helping at all next season — or know organizations or individuals who might! — please contact us as soon as possible.

The cost of each event varies depending on ticket prices, available discounts and transportation costs, but each generally costs between $650 and $3,000.


what inspired PINNACLE OF THE ARTS?


It all began with our New York Arts Adventure, where we took eight arts students to New York City for one week over spring break to experience the pinnacle of their arts and learn directly from world-class professionals in the city.

The week included five world-class theatrical or musical performances; backstage tours and post-show conversations with Broadway casts; and long conversations over lunch with accomplished professionals like theater producer Jessie Austrian, Tony nominee Andy Grotelueschen and theater critic Peter Marks. We also included a visit to the Museum of Modern Art and explored street art with a private tour and hands-on graffiti workshop.

Pinnacle of the Arts was created to make similar experiences available to many more JM students each year. Up to 180 students can attend at least one event each season.
